questions.topic: A binomial probability computed directly
questions.stem: Item 0001 asks a legal clerk to compute a binomial probability directly.

options.text: Use C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k).
Use p^k only.
Use (1-p)^k p^(n-k).
Use n p.

questions.explanation: A direct binomial probability counts arrangements and weights successes and failures.

questions.topic: A Poisson model and the process it describes
questions.stem: Item 0002 asks a clerk to review a Poisson process claim.

options.text: Poisson requires a fixed number of trials.
Poisson models rare independent events over time or space.
Poisson counts successes in a fixed sample size.
Poisson needs two equally likely outcomes.

questions.explanation: Poisson describes event counts in a fixed interval when events are rare and independent.

questions.topic: The central limit theorem and the sample mean
questions.stem: Item 0003 asks a legal clerk to explain the central limit theorem.

answer.exemplar: The central limit theorem says the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately normal as sample size grows, even if the population is not normal.

questions.explanation: Large samples make the sample mean's distribution approximately normal regardless of population shape.

questions.topic: A binomial distribution and its four conditions
questions.stem: Item 0004 asks a clerk to compute P(X=2) if n=5 and p=0.3.

questions.topic: An exponential distribution
questions.stem: Item 0005 asks a clerk to compute P(X>2) if rate=0.5.
questions.explanation: For an exponential distribution, P(X>x) = e^{-lambda x} = e^{-1} = 0.3679.

questions.topic: A chi-squared goodness-of-fit test
questions.stem: Item 0006 asks a clerk to explain a goodness-of-fit test.

options.text: It estimates a population mean.
It tests whether two variables are independent.
It compares observed counts with expected counts under a model.
It requires normally distributed raw data.

questions.explanation: Goodness-of-fit compares observed category counts with counts expected under a hypothesised distribution.

questions.topic: A correlation and what its size indicates
questions.stem: Item 0007 asks a clerk to interpret a correlation size.

options.text: r measures causal strength.
r near 0 indicates strong linear association.
Only positive r indicates association.
Larger absolute r indicates stronger linear association.

questions.explanation: The absolute value of r indicates strength of linear association, regardless of sign.

questions.topic: A hypergeometric model and its sampling assumption
questions.stem: Item 0008 asks a clerk to review a hypergeometric claim.

options.text: Hypergeometric samples with replacement.
Hypergeometric samples without replacement from a finite population.
Hypergeometric requires an infinite population.
Hypergeometric counts events over time.

questions.explanation: Hypergeometric models successes when sampling without replacement from a finite population.

questions.topic: A normal approximation to a binomial count
questions.stem: Item 0009 asks a clerk to explain normal approximation to a binomial count.

answer.exemplar: A normal approximation works when n is large and p is not too close to 0 or 1, so the binomial shape is roughly symmetric.

questions.explanation: Large n and moderate p make the binomial distribution approximately normal.

questions.topic: A gamma distribution and the process it describes
questions.stem: Item 0010 asks a clerk to compute the mean if shape=4 and rate=2.
questions.explanation: Gamma mean = shape/rate = 4/2 = 2.

questions.topic: An exponential distribution and its memoryless property
questions.stem: Item 0011 asks a clerk to compute P(X>5 | X>2) if rate=0.5.
questions.explanation: By memorylessness, P(X>5 | X>2) = P(X>3) = e^{-0.5*3} = 0.2231.

questions.topic: A confidence interval for a mean and its interpretation
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a confidence interval for a mean
questions.stem: Item 0012 asks a clerk to interpret a confidence interval for a mean.

options.text: It guarantees the population mean is inside.
It gives the probability that the sample mean is in the interval.
It gives plausible values for the population mean.
It is a prediction interval for one observation.

questions.explanation: A confidence interval estimates plausible values for the population mean, not a probability about a fixed interval.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II error
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish Type I and Type II errors
questions.stem: Item 0013 asks a clerk to distinguish Type I and Type II errors.

options.text: Neither error depends on the null hypothesis.
Type I misses a false null; Type II rejects a true null.
Both errors are the same mistake.
Type I rejects a true null; Type II misses a false null.

questions.explanation: Type I and Type II errors are opposite mistakes relative to the true state of the null.

questions.topic: A p-value and what it does not mean
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a p-value does not mean
questions.stem: Item 0014 asks a clerk to review a p-value claim.

options.text: A p-value is the probability the null is true.
A p-value is not the probability the null is true.
A p-value is the probability of replication.
A p-value measures effect size.

questions.explanation: A p-value assumes the null is true and measures how extreme the data are, not the probability of the null.

questions.topic: A geometric distribution and what it counts
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a geometric distribution counts
questions.stem: Item 0015 asks a clerk to explain a geometric distribution.

answer.exemplar: A geometric distribution counts the number of independent Bernoulli trials needed to get the first success.

questions.explanation: It models waiting time until the first success in repeated independent trials.

questions.topic: A hypothesis test and the decision rule
questions.learningObjective: State a hypothesis test decision rule
questions.stem: Item 0016 asks a clerk to state the common significance level alpha.
questions.explanation: A common decision threshold is alpha = 0.05.

questions.topic: Power and the sample-size effect
questions.stem: Item 0017 asks a clerk to compute the standard error ratio if sample size quadruples.
questions.explanation: Standard error scales as 1/sqrt(n), so quadrupling n halves it: 1/2 = 0.5.

questions.topic: An F distribution and its use
questions.learningObjective: Explain use of an F distribution
questions.stem: Item 0018 asks a clerk to explain an F distribution.

options.text: It models counts of events.
It tests a single population mean.
It compares variances or mean squares in ANOVA.
It is symmetric around zero.

questions.explanation: F distributions arise from ratios of variances or mean squares, notably in ANOVA.

questions.topic: A chi-squared independence test and its expected counts
questions.stem: Item 0019 asks a clerk to compute an expected count.

options.text: Use the grand total divided by number of cells.
Add row and column totals, then divide by 2.
Use the observed count directly.
Multiply row and column totals, then divide by grand total.

questions.explanation: Under independence, expected count = (row total * column total) / grand total.
questions.hint: Row total times column total over grand total.

questions.topic: A test of variance and its assumption
questions.stem: Item 0020 asks a clerk to review a variance test claim.

options.text: A variance test works for any distribution.
A variance test assumes the underlying population is normal.
A variance test needs no assumptions.
A variance test assumes equal sample sizes.

questions.explanation: Tests of variance are sensitive to non-normality, so normality is a key assumption.

questions.topic: A claim about a p-value that a power calculation contradicts
questions.learningObjective: Explain power contradiction of p-value claim
questions.stem: Item 0021 asks a clerk to explain a p-value claim contradicted by power.

answer.exemplar: A nonsignificant p-value does not prove no effect when power is low, because the study may have been unable to detect the effect.

questions.explanation: Low power means a real effect can fail to reach significance, so absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

questions.topic: A regression coefficient and its interpretation
questions.stem: Item 0022 asks a clerk to predict y if y=2+3x and x=4.
questions.explanation: Substitute x=4: 2 + 3*4 = 14.

questions.topic: A binomial probability computed by summation
questions.stem: Item 0023 asks a clerk to compute P(X<=1) if n=4 and p=0.5.

questions.topic: A residual and the assumption a large one violates
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a large residual violates
questions.stem: Item 0024 asks a clerk to explain a large residual.

options.text: A large residual is always acceptable.
A large residual proves the data are wrong.
A large residual suggests the model may be inadequate.
A large residual means correlation is 1.

questions.explanation: Large residuals indicate the model may miss structure, though they can also arise from outliers.

questions.topic: A moving average and what it smooths
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a moving average smooths
questions.stem: Item 0025 asks a clerk to explain a moving average.

options.text: It counts the number of observations.
It removes all trend information.
It predicts future values exactly.
It smooths short-term fluctuations to reveal trend.

questions.explanation: A moving average averages nearby values, reducing noise to highlight longer-term trend.

questions.topic: A correlation and what its sign and size indicate
questions.learningObjective: Interpret sign and size of correlation
questions.stem: Item 0026 asks a clerk to review a correlation claim.

options.text: Sign gives strength and magnitude gives direction.
Sign gives direction and magnitude gives strength.
Negative correlation means no association.
Correlation sign determines causation.

questions.explanation: The sign indicates direction of association, while absolute magnitude indicates strength.

questions.topic: A nonlinear relationship
questions.stem: Item 0027 asks a clerk to explain a nonlinear relationship.

answer.exemplar: A nonlinear relationship has a changing rate of change, so its graph curves and a straight-line model is inadequate.

questions.explanation: Curvature means the effect of x on y varies across values of x.

questions.topic: A trend line and the residual series it leaves
questions.stem: Item 0028 asks a clerk to compute the moving average of 3, 5, and 7.
questions.explanation: The average is (3+5+7)/3 = 15/3 = 5.

questions.topic: An exponential trend and the rate it implies
questions.stem: Item 0029 asks a clerk to compute the annual rate if a value grows from 200 to 260 over 3 years.

questions.topic: A time series and its components
questions.stem: Item 0030 asks a clerk to identify time series components.

options.text: Only the mean exists.
Only random noise exists.
Trend, seasonal, and irregular components.
Only outliers matter.

questions.explanation: Time series are commonly decomposed into trend, seasonal, and irregular components.
